newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-FOUNDERS WELCOME CHANGES IN EUROPEAN CUP.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FOUNDERS WELCOME CHANGES IN EUROPEAN CUP.

text.p: The French sports daily L'Equipe which created the European Cup in 1955, gave a cautious welcome to the to the expansion of the Champions League announced on Thursday.
"Here we are then ... contemplating a Champions' League that belies its name, because a `non-champion' can win it," L'Equipe said in an editorial on Friday.

It added that the new Champions' League format officially announced by European soccer's governing body UEFA on Thursday would drastically change attitudes towards finishing second in a major league championship.

But it said such a change was inevitable in the modern financial climate in sport, perhaps even an "obligatory stage on the way to a takeover of absolute power by the big clubs and the feeding milk-cows that are the television (channels)."

L'Equipe said despite its expansion the new League, by using the same number of dates in the season, did not disrupt domestic competitions and was fair by including all the continent's champion clubs, even if not all at the same time.
"Since we have to live in our times, welcome to this big baby which already turns our beady eye to second place in our championship with a completely new and excited perspective."

UEFA have increased the Champions' League from 16 to 24 teams from next season, to be played in six groups of four teams, with the six group winners and the two best runners-up progressing to a knock-out stage.
At present teams play in four groups of four with two sides from each group qualifying for the quarter-finals.

UEFA, who dumped champions from smaller nations out of the European Cup two years ago, said the decision to change the format meant all domestic champions would have a chance to qualify for the Champions' League.

The European Cup was launched with eight clubs in 1955 and, though it quickly grew bigger, it only took on a dramatically different aspect with the introduction of the Champions' League in an eight-team format in 1992.
In introducing a second participant from each country, the European Cup is in fact years behind its South American equivalent, the Copa Libertadores.
First played in 1960, the Copa swelled in 1966 to include runners-up on the instigation of the Uruguayan club Penarol.

The Uruguayans were looking to ensure they took part every year: easy in a small first division in which the two big fish, Penarol and Nacional -- like Rangers and Celtic in Scotland -- almost always finished first and second.
Nowadays, countries have various ways of entering teams into the Copa Libertadores, as league runners-up, winners of a playoff round or winners of two separate domestic championships.
